reviewedMergedMetadata.name: Egypt
reviewedMergedMetadata.summary: The kingdom of the Nile, unified around 3100 BCE and ruled by pharaohs for nearly three thousand years. The pyramids of Giza and the Step Pyramid at Saqqara belong to its Old Kingdom; hieroglyphic writing on papyrus, a 365-day civil calendar, monumental temples and the belief in a judged afterlife run through the whole span.

fell.text: Cambyses II of Persia defeated the last king of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty at Pelusium in 525 BCE and Egypt became a Persian province, with native rule returning only in brief intervals until Alexander.

reviews.geometryReason: No political boundary evidence or geometry reconstruction supplied. Existing geometry is unverified source snapshots; acceptance of prose does not verify it.
reviews.narrativeScope: The eight new cultural items and overview are supported. The inherited conquest footer needs explicit phase framing; this is not a completed history of Egypt.

reviewedMergedMetadata.name: Kingdom of Kush
reviewedMergedMetadata.summary: The Nubian kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt, ruled first from Napata and then from Meroë. Its kings ruled Egypt itself as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and Meroë became a center of iron working with its own alphabetic script.

fell.text: Meroë declined as trade routes shifted to the Red Sea; an Aksumite campaign around 350 marks its conventional end.

reviewedMergedMetadata.name: Kingdom of Aksum
reviewedMergedMetadata.summary: A trading kingdom in the Ethiopian highlands, minting its own gold coins and raising monolithic stelae over thirty meters tall. Aksum adopted Christianity around 330 under King Ezana, one of the first states to do so, and wrote in the Ge'ez script still used in Ethiopian liturgy.

fell.text: Red Sea trade passed to Arab merchants and the capital was abandoned; the Zagwe dynasty took over the highlands.
